title: Context Selection Checklist
summary: An intermediate checklist for selecting high-signal context and testing whether the selected material supports the intended task. It includes remediation when required information is missing or results are sensitive to information placement.
prerequisites: A defined task and intended output
The candidate material that could be included as context
Success criteria for evaluating the resulting output

sections.title: What context should I include?
paragraphs: Include the smallest set of high-signal material that supplies the information and constraints needed for the intended outcome. This is an intermediate checklist: it assumes that you already have a defined task, candidate material, and success criteria.

sections.callout: Do not interpret a large available context capacity as a requirement to fill it. No universal token limit, ordering rule, or guaranteed placement behavior is established by the cited sources.

sections.title: Context selection checklist
paragraphs: Check 1: State the task, intended output, and success criteria before selecting context. If any of these cannot be stated, pause selection and ask the requester to clarify the missing requirement rather than guessing.

Check 2: For each candidate item, identify the task requirement, fact, constraint, or example it supports. If an item has no identifiable role, exclude it from the working context or retain it separately for a comparison test.

Check 3: Confirm that the selected material contains the information needed to complete the task. If required information is absent, obtain an authoritative source, ask the requester for the missing material, or narrow the task so that it can be completed from the available evidence.

Check 4: Remove duplication and material that does not contribute to the intended outcome. If relevance is uncertain, compare results with and without that material against the same success criteria; retain it only when the comparison provides evidence that it is useful.

Check 5: Test whether the output changes when important information appears in different positions. Lost in the Middle reports that performance can vary with the position of relevant information, but it does not establish a universal ordering rule. If the test exposes placement sensitivity, reduce competing material, make the relevant instruction or evidence easier to locate, and repeat the test. If sensitivity persists, split the task into smaller stages or require human review of the affected output.

sections.title: Expected evidence and verification
paragraphs: Expected evidence is a traceable selection in which every included item supports a stated task requirement, fact, constraint, or example, while every known required input is either present or recorded as missing.

Verify the selection by running the task against the stated success criteria. Where placement could matter, repeat the test with the relevant information in meaningfully different positions and record whether the result remains acceptable. This test checks for sensitivity in the particular task and context; it does not prove that every model or task behaves the same way.

If the output omits required information, conflicts with supplied evidence, or changes unacceptably across placement tests, the verification has failed. Return to the failed checklist item, add or clarify missing evidence, remove competing material, or divide the task into smaller stages, then repeat verification. If no tested selection meets the success criteria, stop and record the result as unresolved rather than treating the output as verified.
